english_translation: We will leave on time so that we are not late to start our morning meeting.

dialogue.shona: Tichabuda nenguva kuti tisazononoka kutanga musangano wedu wemangwanani.
dialogue.english: We will leave on time so that we are not late to start our morning meeting.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Tichabuda [we will buda] • nenguva [and / with nguva] • kuti [that / so that] • tisazononoka [tisazononoka] • kutanga [to / at tanga] • musangano [in / singular sangano] • wedu [wedu] • wemangwanani [wemangwanani]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Future with '-cha-' ('Tichabuda')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'Tichabuda' in this sentence. Whenever you want to say what 'will' happen in the future, simply place the future marker '-cha-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem. For example, 'ndichabika' means 'I will cook', 'tichasvika' means 'we will arrive', and 'mvura ichanaya' means 'the rain will fall'. Pair it with 'mangwana' ('tomorrow') to talk about tomorrow's plans!
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -cha- + Verb Stem = Future ('will') -> Ndichaenda (I will go), Vachadzoka (They will return)

grammar_notes.title: Connecting Clauses & Expressing Purpose with 'kuti'
grammar_notes.content: The connector 'kuti' is one of the most useful words in Shona. After verbs of speaking, thinking, or knowing (like 'akati' = said, 'unofunga' = you think, 'ndinoziva' = I know), 'kuti' means 'that'. However, when placed after an action verb, 'kuti' means 'so that / in order to', and the following verb changes its final vowel from '-a' to '-e'! For instance, '-dya' (eat) becomes 'kuti tidye' ('so that we may eat'), and '-wana' (get) becomes 'kuti uwane' ('so that you may get').
grammar_notes.rule: kuti + [Subject Prefix + Verb ending in -e] = 'so that [someone] may...' (e.g., kuti tidye = so that we eat)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('wedu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'wedu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).

cultural_notes.title: Early Morning Departures ('Kubuda Nenguva') to Beat Commuter Traffic
cultural_notes.content: In cities like Harare and Bulawayo, commuters set out early from home ('kubuda nenguva') to catch morning transport and arrive ahead of schedule for early-morning workplace meetings.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you politely ask someone to speak softly ('taura zvinyoronyoro')?
In 'Uya kuno undibatsire', what does the prefix '-ndi-' inside 'undibatsire' mean?
active_exercises.explanation: The object prefix '-ndi-' always means 'me', placed directly before the verb stem '-batsira' (help).

active_exercises.explanation: 'Parutivi pe-' means 'beside / at the side of', and 'mugwagwa' is 'road'.
